climbing_route.label: Southeast face gully
climbing_route.notes: Steep scree-and-talus gully splitting Bryant's southeast face, entered at its mouth past a talus field below the rock spire known locally as "the Thumbtack". Ascend favoring its far climber's-right side, which has noticeably firmer footing than the loose center and left. This is the drainage backcountry skiers call the "Bryant Couloir"/"wonder gully" and it is an active avalanche path in winter and spring — avoid it in unstable snow or soon after a storm; axe and crampons if it still holds snow.

climbing_route.label: Bryant-Chair connecting ridge
climbing_route.notes: The gully tops out on the Bryant-Chair connecting ridge; from there work south over blocky ridge and talus to the base of the summit block.

climbing_route.label: Summit block
climbing_route.notes: If the block still holds snow the final scramble is easy Class 3 with little real exposure. In bare/dry conditions the only reasonable line is around the north (climber's left) side on exposed, distinctly loose Class 3 rock — test every hold. Summit 5,790 ft.

climbing_route.label: Saddle to summit
climbing_route.notes: From the broad saddle near 6,800 ft (also the junction with the climbers'/unmaintained Rock Creek Trail heading east), bear left and switchback up open talus and scree for a final 0.4-0.5 mile to the summit at 7,091 ft, passing near a minor false high point. Class 1-2 the entire way — a steep trail/talus walk, no technical scrambling. Snow can linger on the upper switchbacks and around the saddle into early-mid July and an ice axe is worth carrying for those patches; the exposed saddle/ridge can be windy. The only route-finding subtlety up here is staying on-trail through the talus near the summit block.

climbing_route.label: Buttress step above 6,300 ft
climbing_route.notes: Above roughly 6,300 ft the route works past a buttress via one of two class 3-4 options: a crack/chimney move on the left, or an easier move right into a ~50-ft gully. This short section has minimal exposure. Route-finding through the boulder fields and buttress is the main crux.

climbing_route.label: ~50-ft gully
climbing_route.notes: The gully above the buttress is steep with loose rock — parties should stay close together and wear helmets.

climbing_route.label: Southwest face slabs and scree
climbing_route.notes: Above the gully, class 2-3 slabs and scree lead across the southwest face to the base of the summit block. Snow lingering into early summer on the upper ledges makes the route significantly more hazardous; best attempted after it has melted out.

climbing_route.label: Summit block corkscrew
climbing_route.notes: Finish with a short class 3 corkscrew move around the final cliff band to the top.

climbing_route.label: South-facing slopes to the summit gully
climbing_route.notes: From Foggy Lake (~5,200 ft), cross the boulder field on climbers' trail along the lake's north side, then ascend Del Campo's south-facing slopes toward ~6,200 ft, aiming for the main summit gully.

climbing_route.label: Exit left of the gully to the col
climbing_route.notes: Route-finding caution: the obvious gully looks like the natural line but ends in a vertical wall. The actual route exits the gully and moves onto class 3-4 rock just left of it about 100 vertical feet below the top, working up to a notch/col at roughly 6,350 ft. A helmet is strongly recommended for the loose upper rock.

climbing_route.label: Final pitch from the col
climbing_route.notes: From the col, turn west/left and scramble the final short pitch to the true summit (6,610-6,615 ft). Snow can linger in the gully and basin into early September.

climbing_route.label: Point 8207
climbing_route.notes: From the tarn near 7,400'/col, regain the crest and follow it north. Point 8207 is the technical crux of the traverse — exposed class 3-4 scrambling on otherwise solid rock.

climbing_route.label: Point 8165
climbing_route.notes: Sustained class 3 moves and one exposed, improbable-looking ledge traverse through a small cliff band; most parties bypass Pt 8165's true summit to the west.

climbing_route.label: Summit crest walk-up
climbing_route.notes: Beyond Pt 8165 the ridge relents into a pleasant, mostly-dirt walk above treeline, and Dot Mountain's summit is reached by an easy, non-technical walk-up along the crest. No water anywhere on this high ridge traverse until a small tarn on Ptarmigan Peak's south shoulder, well beyond Dot Mountain.

climbing_route.label: South-side talus-and-scree gully
climbing_route.notes: From camp in upper Phelps Basin (~6,000 ft), leave the last of the boot path and head east/northeast up along a tumbling side creek that cuts through an otherwise cliffy face, following a broad talus-and-scree gully on the south side of Dumbell. Grass and heather give way to talus and, through roughly mid-August, moderate snow as you climb into the basin directly south of the summit. A reported unstable, truck-sized snow block is perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully.

climbing_route.label: Gully west of the notch to the ledges
climbing_route.notes: Gain the southeast ridge/shoulder at a distinct notch, then work up steep snow or a loose scree-and-talus gully 100-200 yards left (west) of the notch to reach a system of ledges. Route-finding is the main crux — several parallel gullies and ledge systems exist and it's easy to get cliffed out on the wrong one; loose rock and lingering steep snow (ice axe and sometimes crampons into July) are real hazards.

climbing_route.label: West ridge
climbing_route.notes: The ledges zig-zag up onto the west ridge, which is then followed a few hundred feet of easy but moderately exposed Class 3 scrambling to the 8,421-ft summit.

climbing_route.label: South-facing gullies to the Eye Col
climbing_route.notes: From the basin camp below Mount Terror (~6,050'), descend about 300' below the moraine to the head of Crescent Creek, then work up and around buttresses toward the braided, loose south-facing gullies beneath the Eye Col, the notch separating East and West Twin Needle. The final few hundred feet to the col involve steep, loose gully climbing with real route-finding uncertainty — this south side has comparatively sparse route information and can feel disorienting in cloud or low light.

climbing_route.label: Southeast ridge / east arete
climbing_route.notes: From the Eye Col, gain the exposed southeast ridge/east arete, which the route follows to the summit.

wa_forbidden_peak_northeast_face.skip_reason: The approach text stops exactly at the base of the Northeast Face below a prominent ice patch and describes none of the face itself. The technical passages it does name (the ~10 ft of 5.7 rock and Class 3 gully to Sharkfin Col, the rappel into the bergschrund, the short ice wall onto the Boston Glacier, and the westward Boston Glacier traverse) are all genuine approach features en route to the base, not segments of the Northeast Face route, so re-homing them would misdescribe the climb.
